subject: botany
question_text: Which division is necessary to maintain a constant chromosome number in all the body cells of a multicellular organism, and why?

mark_split.label: All body cells come from the zygote

page_header: Cell Cycle and Cell Division · 4 marks

steps.label: The division named
lines: Mitosis is the division that keeps the
chromosome number constant in all body cells.
It is also called the equational division, because
each daughter cell ends with the same number of
chromosomes as the mother cell (2n → 2n).
steps.why: The question has two halves, and the first mark is simply for naming mitosis and the word equational. Answer the 'which' before you start on the 'why'.
common_mistakes: Naming meiosis. Meiosis halves the number and happens only in reproductive tissue.
steps.memory_tip: Mitosis is equational: 2n gives 2n. Meiosis is reductional: 2n gives n.
steps.margin_note: Name it in the first line. The rest of the answer is the reason.

steps.label: One replication, one division
lines: DNA is replicated once, in the S phase, so each
chromosome now has two sister chromatids
joined at one centromere.
At anaphase the centromere divides and one
chromatid of every chromosome goes to each
pole.
So each daughter nucleus receives one full set:
the number is neither doubled nor halved.
steps.why: One round of replication followed by one division is the arithmetic that keeps the number the same. Doubling the material and then splitting it once returns each daughter cell to the starting number.
common_mistakes: Saying the chromosome number doubles in S phase. Only the DNA amount doubles.
Leaving out the centromere division. Without it the chromatids could not be shared equally.
steps.memory_tip: Double once, divide once. That is why the number comes back to where it started.
steps.margin_note: Three short lines: replication, centromere division, result.

steps.label: Identical daughter cells
lines: Homologous chromosomes do not pair and there
is no crossing over in mitosis.
The two daughter cells are therefore genetically
identical to each other and to the mother cell, in
both quality and quantity.
steps.why: Mitosis has no pairing and no exchange, and that is exactly why it copies rather than reshuffles. This contrast with meiosis is what the examiner is looking for.
common_mistakes: Writing that crossing over occurs in mitosis.
Saying the daughter cells are 'similar'. The word wanted is identical.
steps.memory_tip: No pairing, no crossing over, no variation. Mitosis copies; meiosis mixes.
steps.margin_note: Two lines. State the contrast with meiosis in plain words.

steps.label: All body cells come from the zygote

lines.text: Mitosis — every body cell is derived from the zygote by repeated mitosis, so all of them carry the zygote's chromosome number.

lines: That is how a whole multicellular body, built from
one fertilised egg, ends with the same 2n in
every cell.
steps.why: The final mark is for closing the argument: a constant number in EVERY body cell follows only if every body cell traces back to one cell by a division that does not change the number.
common_mistakes: Stopping at 'mitosis gives identical cells' without linking it back to the zygote.
steps.memory_tip: One zygote, many mitoses, one chromosome number throughout the body.
steps.margin_note: Close with the zygote sentence. It is the sentence that answers 'why in ALL body cells'.

insider_note: The question says 'and why', so half the marks are in the reason. A one-word answer of 'mitosis' scores one mark out of four.
